variants.name: Expression trees translated by LINQ/EF Core
variants.implementation_notes: The .NET realization treats the rule as data: a specification exposes Expression<Func<T,bool>>, composition combines bodies with Expression.AndAlso/OrElse/Not (rebinding the right-hand parameter to the left-hand one with an ExpressionVisitor), and IQueryable providers such as EF Core translate the resulting tree into SQL while a cached .Compile() gives the in-memory check from the same definition. Plain Func<T,bool>/Predicate<T> delegates are the alternative whenever the rule never leaves memory: cheaper, but opaque, so the rule cannot be inspected, logged or translated. Libraries such as Ardalis.Specification package exactly this split (expression for IQueryable, compiled delegate for IEnumerable); a hand-written ISpecification<T> is still warranted when specifications must also carry include/order/paging metadata, at which point they become query objects as much as rules.
pitfalls: Merging two Expression<Func<T,bool>> without rebinding the parameter throws at query time ('variable ... referenced from scope ... but it is not defined'); a visitor that replaces the right-hand ParameterExpression is mandatory.

Expression trees cannot contain statement lambdas, await, many newer C# constructs or arbitrary method calls; a rule that compiles can still fail when the provider translates it, so test against the real provider.
Compile once and cache the delegate: compiling per candidate is dramatically slower than the evaluation itself.
Capturing a mutable variable (DateTime.UtcNow, a changing request object) hides the parameter in the tree; pass values in as constants or constructor arguments.

variants.name: In-memory delegates (Func<T,bool> / Predicate<T>)
variants.implementation_notes: When the rule is only ever evaluated in memory, model it as a delegate: a lambda or method group of type Func<T,bool> (or Predicate<T> for API compatibility), composed with local functions or the static helpers on System.Predicate, and consumed by Enumerable.Where/Any/All. This is the cheapest realization and needs no Expression visitor, but it cannot be inspected, serialized or translated: passing it to an IQueryable filters nothing at the database, and rendering it back to a query means restating the rule in the provider's dialect.
pitfalls: Delegates are opaque: no logging, serialization or translation, and a delegate accidentally applied to IQueryable via IEnumerable both filters client-side and loads every row.
Closure capture makes the rule read mutable state at evaluation time; capture the values the rule needs when the delegate is created.
Delegate equality is reference-based, so delegate-based specifications cannot be compared or deduplicated; use an expression tree or a named class when identity matters.
